title: Counting Blasts: The MDS–AML Line and the APL Emergency
summary: Learn which cells count as blasts, where the WHO 2022 and ICC 2022 classifications draw the lines between MDS and AML, how defining genetic abnormalities change the blast threshold, and why suspected acute promyelocytic leukemia is treated with ATRA before genetic confirmation.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 34 Hits 2 (APL emergency, ATRA, immunophenotype), 3 (AML ≥20% blasts and genetic exceptions) and 6 (MDS criteria), and Traps 3 (APL below 20%) and 5 (blast equivalents). Checked against the WHO 2022 myeloid classification (Khoury 2022), the ICC 2022 (Arber 2022; read via a page-fetch tool), the ELN APL recommendations (Sanz 2019; read via a page-fetch tool), Yilmaz 2021 and Gurnari 2021. Differences from the reviewer: MDS cytopenia thresholds are Hb <13/<12 g/dL, ANC <1.8 and platelets <150 ×10⁹/L in both 2022 classifications, not Hb <10 and platelets <100 (register flag rv-mds-cytopenia-2022); WHO 2022 renames EB1/EB2 as IB1/IB2, defines the SF3B1 type by the mutation with ≥15% ring sideroblasts as a substitute, and ICC 2022 calls 10–19% blasts MDS/AML (rv-mds-eb-ib-terminology); the genetic exception to the 20% rule is classification-dependent and broader than APL and inv(16) in WHO 2022 (rv-aml-genetic-cutoff-ch34). Not taught as fact: the 500-cell differential, the inv(16) karyotype notation, progression percentages.

objectives: List the cells counted as blasts or blast equivalents in myeloid neoplasms.
Place a marrow blast percentage on the WHO 2022 MDS–AML ladder and state how ICC 2022 differs.
Recognise suspected APL from morphology, coagulation results and immunophenotype, and state the immediate action.

scenes.title: Three marrows, one line
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three bone-marrow reports. (1) 12% myeloblasts plus 10% promonocytes; (2) 25% blasts, no Auer rods, normal karyotype; (3) 14% abnormal hypergranular promyelocytes with Auer rods in a patient who is bleeding, with low fibrinogen and low platelets. Question token: “MDS, AML, or an emergency?”

cues.text: Three marrow reports arrive. The first has twelve percent myeloblasts plus ten percent promonocytes. The second has twenty-five percent blasts and a normal karyotype.
The third has fourteen percent abnormal promyelocytes packed with Auer rods, in a patient who is bleeding with low fibrinogen.
Which is myelodysplasia, which is acute myeloid leukemia, and which is an emergency right now?

scenes.title: What counts as a blast, and the 20% line
scenes.altText: Schematic cards. Blast equivalents: myeloblasts, monoblasts and promonocytes are counted together as blasts (WHO 2022, ICC 2022); in the right setting, the abnormal promyelocytes of APL are counted as blast equivalents too (ICC 2022). The 20% line: WHO 2022 keeps a 20% blast cutoff to separate MDS from AML. MDS definition: cytopenia plus morphologic dysplasia in at least 10% of the cells of a lineage. Cytopenia (WHO 2022 and ICC 2022): haemoglobin below 13 g/dL in males and below 12 g/dL in females, neutrophils below 1.8 × 10⁹/L, platelets below 150 × 10⁹/L.

cues.text: First, decide what counts as a blast. Myeloblasts, monoblasts and promonocytes are all counted together as blasts.
In acute promyelocytic leukemia, the abnormal promyelocytes count as blast equivalents too.
The 2022 WHO classification keeps a twenty percent blast line between myelodysplastic neoplasm and acute myeloid leukemia.

Myelodysplasia itself needs cytopenia plus dysplasia in at least ten percent of a lineage’s cells. In the 2022 definitions, cytopenia means haemoglobin below thirteen in men or twelve in women, neutrophils below one point eight, or platelets below one hundred fifty.

props.title: MDS = cytopenia + dysplasia ≥ 10% of a lineage

scenes.title: The blast ladder and the genetic shortcut
scenes.altText: Ladder card (WHO 2022 MDS): low blasts = under 5% marrow and under 2% blood; MDS-IB1 = 5–9% marrow or 2–4% blood; MDS-IB2 = 10–19% marrow or 5–19% blood or Auer rods; 20% or more = AML. ICC 2022 instead calls 10–19% blasts MDS/AML. MDS with SF3B1 mutation is a LOW-blast type; 15% or more ring sideroblasts may substitute for the mutation. Genetic card: WHO 2022 removed the 20% requirement for most AML with defining genetic abnormalities (APL with PML::RARA among them), except AML with BCR::ABL1 and AML with CEBPA mutation; morphology must correlate. ICC 2022 requires at least 10% blasts for these, and 20% for BCR::ABL1.

cues.text: Now climb the ladder. Under five percent marrow blasts is low-blast myelodysplasia. Five to nine percent is increased blasts one, and ten to nineteen percent, or Auer rods, is increased blasts two. Twenty percent is acute leukemia.
The rival 2022 International Consensus Classification calls ten to nineteen percent MDS/AML. And ring sideroblasts or an SF3B1 mutation define a low-blast type: they do not cancel a high blast count.

Genetics can override the headcount. The 2022 WHO classification removed the twenty percent requirement for most AML types with a defining genetic abnormality, including APL with PML::RARA. AML with BCR::ABL1 or a CEBPA mutation still needs twenty percent.
The International Consensus Classification sets ten percent for these genetic types instead. Either way, an APL fusion with fourteen percent abnormal promyelocytes is acute leukemia.

scenes.title: Spotting APL and acting first
scenes.altText: APL cards. Morphology: hypergranular promyelocytes with Auer rods, often bundled (“faggot cells”); microgranular variant exists. Coagulopathy: prolonged PT and PTT, high D-dimer, low fibrinogen and low platelets in about three-quarters of patients at diagnosis; intracerebral and pulmonary haemorrhage are the main causes of death. Flow: bright CD33, HLA-DR, CD34 and CD11b absent or low, CD13 and CD117 heterogeneous, MPO positive; the microgranular variant often expresses CD34 and CD2. Action: start ATRA as soon as APL is suspected; confirm PML::RARA molecularly; stop ATRA if not confirmed; transfuse to keep fibrinogen above 100 mg/dL and platelets above 30 × 10⁹/L; avoid invasive procedures. Hook answers: (1) 22% blasts plus equivalents = AML; (2) 25% = AML; (3) suspected APL: emergency treatment while PML::RARA is confirmed.

cues.text: Recognise APL. Abnormal hypergranular promyelocytes carry Auer rods, often in bundles called faggot cells. About three quarters of patients have a consumptive coagulopathy at diagnosis: long PT and PTT, high D-dimer, low fibrinogen and low platelets.
Flow cytometry shows bright CD33, with HLA-DR, CD34 and CD11b absent or low, and myeloperoxidase positive. The microgranular variant often expresses CD34, so do not rule APL out on CD34 alone.

Start all-trans retinoic acid as soon as APL is suspected, confirm PML::RARA by molecular testing, and stop it if APL is not confirmed. Support the coagulopathy with transfusions and avoid invasive procedures.
Back to the hook. Marrow one has twenty-two percent blasts plus equivalents: AML. Marrow two is AML. Marrow three is suspected APL: treat it as an emergency while PML::RARA is confirmed.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Count only the myeloblasts” (✓ promonocytes, monoblasts and, in APL, abnormal promyelocytes count as blast equivalents); “Ring sideroblasts make it MDS with ring sideroblasts, whatever the blasts” (✓ the SF3B1 / ring-sideroblast type is a low-blast type; 12% blasts is IB2 by WHO 2022 or MDS/AML by ICC 2022); “Wait for PML::RARA before ATRA” (✓ start ATRA on suspicion; stop it if not confirmed).

cues.text: Trap one: count only the myeloblasts. No: promonocytes, monoblasts, and in APL the abnormal promyelocytes, all count toward the blast percentage.

Trap two: ring sideroblasts make it the ring sideroblast type whatever the blast count. No: that is a low-blast type. Twelve percent blasts is increased blasts two, or MDS/AML in the rival classification.
Trap three: wait for the PML::RARA result before giving ATRA. No: start it on suspicion, and stop it if the genetics do not confirm APL.

lines: ✓ SF3B1 / ring sideroblast type is low-blast

scenes.title: Headcount and ID card
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Blasts are a HEADCOUNT, genes are an ID CARD. Count the whole gang (blasts plus equivalents); 20 is the line when no ID card is found; a PML::RARA ID card means sound the alarm at any count.” Tokens: headcount = blasts + equivalents · line = 20% · ID card = defining genetics. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: blasts are a headcount, genes are an ID card. Count the whole gang, blasts plus equivalents. Twenty percent is the line when no ID card turns up, and an APL ID card means sound the alarm at any count.

Where it breaks: the International Consensus Classification still asks for ten percent blasts in genetic types; BCR::ABL1 and CEBPA types still need twenty percent; the genetics must match the morphology; and blast counts vary with sampling and observer.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Blasts + equivalents · 20% line · genetic types lower or no cutoff”, “Suspected APL → ATRA now, confirm PML::RARA, support coagulation”.

cues.text: Count myeloblasts, monoblasts, promonocytes and abnormal promyelocytes together, call acute myeloid leukemia at 20 percent unless a defining genetic abnormality changes the threshold, and treat suspected acute promyelocytic leukemia as an emergency with immediate all-trans retinoic acid.

props.label: Blasts + equivalents · 20% line · genetics can lower it
Suspected APL → ATRA now · confirm PML::RARA · support clotting

explanation.what: Plain language: in myeloid cancers, labs count the very immature cells (blasts). A low count with abnormal-looking cells and low blood counts suggests myelodysplasia; 20% or more means acute leukemia. Some genetic changes mean acute leukemia even with fewer blasts, and one of them, acute promyelocytic leukemia, causes dangerous bleeding and is treated straight away. Scientific terms: blast equivalents (monoblasts, promonocytes, abnormal promyelocytes), myelodysplastic neoplasm (MDS), MDS with increased blasts (IB1, IB2), MDS/AML (ICC), AML with defining genetic abnormalities, PML::RARA, consumptive coagulopathy, all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA).
explanation.why: The blast percentage separates diseases with very different treatment, but any cutoff is arbitrary and counts vary with sampling, so WHO 2022 lets defining genetics override it for most genetic AML types. In APL, the PML::RARA fusion blocks differentiation at the promyelocyte stage, and the coagulopathy causes early haemorrhagic deaths, so ATRA is started on suspicion.
explanation.measure: Count myeloblasts + monoblasts + promonocytes (+ abnormal promyelocytes in APL). WHO 2022: MDS low blasts <5% BM and <2% PB; IB1 5–9% BM or 2–4% PB; IB2 10–19% BM or 5–19% PB or Auer rods; AML ≥20%, or no cutoff for most defining genetic types (except BCR::ABL1 and CEBPA). ICC 2022: MDS/AML 10–19%; genetic AML ≥10% (BCR::ABL1 ≥20%). MDS cytopenia: Hb <13 (M) / <12 (F) g/dL, ANC <1.8, platelets <150 ×10⁹/L; dysplasia ≥10% of a lineage. APL: bright CD33, HLA-DR/CD34/CD11b low or absent; ATRA on suspicion; fibrinogen >100 mg/dL and platelets >30 ×10⁹/L.
explanation.differs: WHO 2022 vs ICC 2022 thresholds; MDS-IB2 vs AML; SF3B1/ring-sideroblast type (low blasts) vs increased blasts; classic APL (CD34 low/absent) vs microgranular variant (often CD34+, CD2+).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: add blast equivalents to reach a diagnosis, choose the immediate step in suspected APL, pick the APL immunophenotype, or place a blast count on the MDS ladder.

questions.stem: A marrow aspirate from a patient with cytopenias shows 12% myeloblasts and 10% promonocytes, with no AML-defining genetic abnormality. How should it be classified under WHO 2022?

options.rationale: Correct. Promonocytes are blast equivalents, so the blast count is 22%, above the 20% line.
Incorrect. That would follow from counting only the 12% myeloblasts; promonocytes must be added.
Incorrect. Low blasts means under 5% marrow blasts.

questions.stem: A bleeding patient has hypergranular promyelocytes with bundles of Auer rods, low fibrinogen and low platelets. PML::RARA testing is pending. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Start all-trans retinoic acid now and support the coagulopathy
options.rationale: Correct. ELN recommends starting ATRA as soon as APL is suspected, with blood-product support; ATRA is stopped if APL is not confirmed.

options.text: Wait for PML::RARA confirmation before any specific treatment
options.rationale: Incorrect. Haemorrhage (intracerebral and pulmonary) is the most frequent cause of death in APL, so ATRA should not wait for the genetic result.

options.text: Do a lumbar puncture first to check the CSF
options.rationale: Incorrect. Invasive procedures such as lumbar puncture should be avoided during the coagulopathy.

options.text: Hold treatment because blasts plus promyelocytes are under 20%
options.rationale: Incorrect. APL with PML::RARA is not held to the 20% rule (no cutoff in WHO 2022, ≥10% in ICC 2022), and suspicion alone justifies ATRA.

questions.stem: Which flow cytometry pattern is characteristic of classic (hypergranular) acute promyelocytic leukemia?

options.text: Bright CD33 with HLA-DR and CD34 absent or low, MPO positive
options.rationale: Correct. This is the classic APL pattern described in reviews of APL immunophenotype.

options.text: Strong HLA-DR and CD34 on most cells
options.rationale: Incorrect. Classic APL shows absent or low HLA-DR and CD34; CD34 is more often seen in the microgranular variant.

options.text: MPO negative with lymphoid markers only
options.rationale: Incorrect. APL is a myeloid leukemia and MPO is positive.
Incorrect. CD11b is absent or low in classic APL, as is HLA-DR.

claims.text: Myeloblasts, monoblasts and promonocytes count as blasts; abnormal promyelocytes count as blast equivalents in APL.
20% blast cutoff between MDS and AML (WHO 2022); remaining AML ≥20% and MDS/AML 10–19% (ICC 2022).
WHO 2022 removed the 20% requirement for most AML with defining genetic abnormalities except BCR::ABL1 and CEBPA; ICC 2022 requires ≥10% (BCR::ABL1 ≥20%).
MDS cytopenia thresholds, 10% dysplasia, IB1/IB2 cutoffs, MDS-SF3B1 as a low-blast type with ≥15% ring sideroblasts as substitute.
APL morphology, coagulopathy pattern and frequency, classic and variant immunophenotype.
ATRA on suspicion, molecular confirmation of PML::RARA, stop if not confirmed, transfusion targets, avoid invasive procedures; PML::RARA blocks differentiation and ATRA-based therapy restores it.
500-cell marrow differential; inv(16) karyotype notation as a blast-count exception; reviewer’s Hb <10 and platelets <100 cytopenia thresholds (older criteria).

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 34 Hit 6 and the Number Vault give MDS cytopenias as Hb <10 g/dL, ANC <1.8 and platelets <100 ×10⁹/L. WHO 2022 (Khoury 2022) and ICC 2022 (Arber 2022) define cytopenia as Hb <13 g/dL (males) / <12 g/dL (females), ANC <1.8 ×10⁹/L and platelets <150 ×10⁹/L (register flag rv-mds-cytopenia-2022).

Ch. 34 Hit 6 uses EB1/EB2 and “ring sideroblasts ≥15% (or ≥5% with SF3B1)”. WHO 2022 renames these MDS-IB1/IB2 (same marrow cutoffs, plus blood criteria and Auer rods for IB2) and defines MDS-SF3B1 by the mutation (a low-blast type) with ≥15% ring sideroblasts as a substitute; ICC 2022 calls 10–19% blasts MDS/AML (register flag rv-mds-eb-ib-terminology).

Ch. 34 Hit 3 and Trap 3 say APL and inv(16) are diagnostic regardless of blast count. That matches WHO 2022 only in part (WHO 2022 removes the cutoff for most defining genetic types, except BCR::ABL1 and CEBPA); ICC 2022 requires ≥10% blasts, including for APL (register flag rv-aml-genetic-cutoff-ch34).
